_comment: Curated A20 test-point data. Hand-authored from the service manuals rather than
parsed. A20 has no supply table of its own and no Chapter 5 section, so the
sources here are three:
1. The sheet 1 test point legend, which names all thirteen points and gives a
page/zone reference for each. Every one of those references was checked by
opening the zone it names; all thirteen agree.
2. Table 2-2, for the three rails A19 delivers to this board on P61/P62.
3. §2-30 to §2-45 and Table 2-3, for the clock frequencies and the thresholds.
There is no TP2. The legend jumps TP1 to TP3, the 1996 list prints 'TP1, TP3-14'
and the Rev 9 list 'TP 1, 3- 12'. That is the numbering, not a gap in this file.
The three supply points carry a value measured somewhere else. Table 2-2 gives
the nominal and tolerance at the *Digital Power Supply's* own test points -- +5 V
at A19's TP12, +12 V at its TP8, -12 V at its TP10 -- and these are the far end
of the same three rails after P61/P62 and the motherboard. Each carries the
table's figure with inferred set, because the drop between the two ends is real
and is published nowhere.
Two things in Table 2-2 would mislead if copied literally, and both are the
pitfalls the pipeline has met before:
- the '-12 VOLTS' row prints its nominal as '12V' with the sign dropped. TP7 is
signed here and says so in conflict.
- the '+5V' row's nominal is 5.2 V, not 5.0 V. That is deliberate: §2-25 says
A19's CR35 raises the regulator's output about 0.2 V. 5.2 V at TP6 is the
published figure and is not a high reading.
Rev 9 lists jumper wires for TP1 and TP3-TP12 only (stock 816090, eleven of
them). TP13 and TP14 appear in the 1996 list's 'TP1, TP3-14' but in no Rev 9 row,
so on this build they are the battery's own solder pads rather than fitted loops;
they carry notInParts and kind 'pad'.
The E-series strapping pads -- E1 (cut to disable the watchdog), E2, E3, E4
(the battery's return to common) and E5 (selects the alternate oscillator) --
are printed on the sheets and etched on the board but appear in neither parts
list, because they are pads rather than purchased parts. They cannot be named
in onFail for that reason, so where one matters it is named in the note
instead: E5 for TP1 and TP3, E4 for TP14.
TP9, TP10, TP11 and TP12 are logic and serial lines the manuals never tabulate.
They carry noPublishedValue rather than an invented number. They are still worth
placing: they are the only points on the board where the fibre-optic link to the
guarded section can be watched without unsoldering anything.

testpoints.condition: Power on, instrument running or held in reset
testpoints.source: §2-32, and the Y1 annotation on sheet 1
testpoints.note: The primary system clock, straight off the Y1 Pierce oscillator through an inverter in U3 and jumper E5. §2-32 states 7.3728 MHz outright and the sheet prints it beside the crystal. The processor's own CLK pin (U8 pin 15) is on this net, so this is the clock the 68HC000 actually runs on. The tolerance is the crystal's: Rev 9 gives Y1 as +-1% and the 1996 part as 50/100 ppm, so 0.01% is the later part's figure and the older one is a hundred times looser -- treat any reading within a few hundred Hz as good. U4 divides this net down to 3.6864 MHz, 28.8 kHz and 450 Hz; if those are absent but this is present, suspect U4 rather than the oscillator.

The 68HC000's E output, pin 20, brought straight out to this point -- the enable clock for 6800-family peripherals. Table 2-3 prints the frequency as part of the signal's own glossary entry: 'E  Enable for 6800 family devices (737.28 kHz clock)'. It is CLK divided by ten inside the processor, so it is also the most direct evidence available that the processor is alive and clocking: TP1 good and TP3 dead means the 68HC000 itself, not the oscillator.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG4C5) and sheet 4
testpoints.note: Digital common, and the reference for every measurement on this board except the battery. TP8 is a second loop on the same net -- two were provided so a meter's low lead and a scope's ground can both be clipped on without sharing one loop.

testpoints.source: Table 2-2, +12 VOLTS row (measured at A19 TP8)
testpoints.note: Generated on the Digital Power Supply (A19) by regulator U1 and delivered here through P61/P62 and the Digital Motherboard. Table 2-2's nominal and tolerance are quoted at A19's own TP8, so the figure is marked inferred at this end: the drop across the motherboard and the connector is real and is published nowhere. On this board the +/-12 V pair supplies only the fan monitor comparators in U52 (§2-45), so a fault here presents as a spurious FANINT* rather than as a dead instrument.

The rail everything on this board runs on, from A19 through P61/P62. The nominal is 5.2 V and not 5.0 V because A19's CR35, a germanium diode in the regulator's ground leg, deliberately lifts the output about 0.2 V (§2-25) -- a reading of 5.2 V here is correct and not high. The number that matters more than the tolerance is U1's threshold: §2-31 says the instrument is held in reset whenever this rail falls below 4.55 V +-0.05 V, so a supply sagging under load gives a dead instrument and a dark CR1 rather than erratic behaviour. Table 2-2's figure is quoted at A19's TP12, hence inferred at this end.

testpoints.source: Table 2-2, -12 VOLTS row (measured at A19 TP10)
testpoints.conflict: Table 2-2 prints this rail's nominal as '12V', unsigned, in the row named '-12 VOLTS'. It is -12 V; the sign is dropped in the printed table, as it is for several rows of Tables 2-8 and 2-9 elsewhere in the manual. Signed here.
testpoints.note: From A19's -12 V regulator through P61/P62. Used on this board only by the fan monitor op-amps in U52, whose comparator outputs swing to about -11 V (§2-45), so this rail sets that swing. Table 2-2's figure is quoted at A19's TP10, hence inferred at this end.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG4C5) and sheet 4
testpoints.note: The second digital common loop, on the same net as TP4.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG5D6) and sheet 5
testpoints.note: TXDB, the DUART's channel B transmit line, on the way into U32 (a 75451) which drives the fibre-optic transmitter on the Digital Motherboard (§2-40). This is the outgoing half of the only link between the unguarded CPU and the guarded digital controller. The manuals tabulate no value; it is a TTL line that should be idle high and show serial activity whenever the instrument talks to the guarded section. Watch it here and RCVB at TP10 together: activity on TP9 with none on TP10 puts the fault beyond the fibre rather than on this board.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG5D6) and sheet 5
testpoints.note: The DUART's channel B receive line, arriving from the fibre-optic receiver through P62. The incoming half of the guard-crossing link, and the counterpart to TP9. No published value; a TTL line idling high.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG5C6) and sheet 5
testpoints.note: §2-40: 'Line SCLK is a test output of the channel A serial clock' -- an output the DUART provides purely so this point can exist. No published frequency, because it follows whatever baud rate the software has programmed into U31.

testpoints.source: Sheet 1 test point legend (PG5B4) and sheet 5
testpoints.conflict: The sheet 1 legend and the sheet 5 net label both read CLKI; the board silkscreen reads CLK1. Table 2-3 has no CLKI or CLK1 entry, but the net this point sits on is CLKCALINT*, the clock/calendar interrupt, so the legend's I is a letter and not a one. Both spellings recorded; the drawings are followed.
testpoints.note: The clock/calendar interrupt line CLKCALINT*, generated by U33 under software control (§2-41) and pulled up to +5 V through Z3. Interrupt priority 4, vector F5 (Table 2-5). Idles high; pulses low when U33 raises an alarm the software has armed.

testpoints.condition: Any -- the cell is live whether the instrument is powered or not
testpoints.note: Straight across BT1, the lithium cell that keeps U33's clock and calendar running with the instrument off (§2-41). The tolerance is this dataset's, not the manual's: a 3 V lithium primary sits near 3.0-3.2 V for almost all of its life and falls off a cliff at the end, so anything below about 2.7 V should be replaced even though it may still keep time. Rev 9 gives the cell as 3.0 V, 0.5 Ah, stock 821439. Replacing it is §4-21 -- it is soldered in on this build -- and it loses the time, the date and the ETIME elapsed-time counter, so read ETIME? first (§4-23).

The battery's negative terminal, and the reference for TP13. It reaches digital common through jumper E4 (JP20 on sheet 5) rather than directly, so it is not simply another ground loop -- do not substitute TP4 for it when measuring the cell.
